Family Health

Vulvovaginitis: causes and care in children and adults

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Vulvovaginitis describes inflammation or irritation involving the vulva and vagina; it is not the name of one infection. The vulva is the external genital area, including the labia and clitoris, rather than only the vaginal opening. Causes and suitable care differ with age, symptoms and circumstances.

Possible causes: infection is not the only explanation

Bacteria, yeast and some sexually transmitted infections can cause symptoms, but so can friction, trapped moisture, soap or other irritants, allergy and skin disorders such as eczema or lichen sclerosus. Lower estrogen before puberty, after menopause or during breastfeeding can affect tissue sensitivity. Do not assume all inflammation is bacterial or apply one prevalence estimate to every age group.

Consider recent medicines, antibiotics, period products, detergents, perfumed sprays, lubricants or spermicides, tight clothing and wet swimwear. A product may irritate one person without being universally harmful; an ingredient list alone does not diagnose an allergy or infection. Gentle care helps reduce irritation without blaming the person’s cleanliness.

Bacterial and yeast conditions

Bacterial vaginosis involves a change in a mixed vaginal bacterial community, including Gardnerella and other organisms, not simply one dangerous bacterium multiplying. Thin grey or white discharge and a fishy smell can occur, but symptoms overlap. Some other bacteria can cause a targeted infection, particularly in children; a positive culture must be interpreted with symptoms and examination.

Candida can cause marked itching, soreness, redness and thick white or sometimes different discharge. Antibiotics can contribute, but symptoms are not proof of yeast and Candida may be present without causing illness. Thrush is unusual between infancy and puberty, so do not automatically give a child an antifungal. Persistent or recurrent adult symptoms may need testing rather than repeated over-the-counter courses.

Sexually transmitted infections, viruses and parasites

Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted parasitic infection and may cause irritation, urinary discomfort and changed discharge, or no symptoms. Chlamydia and gonorrhoea can cause cervicitis and discharge needing different treatment. Herpes may cause painful blisters or ulcers; HPV often has no symptoms or may cause warts, rather than being a usual explanation for general vaginitis. A new sore, growth or suspected STI deserves assessment.

Pinworms can produce troublesome night-time vulval or anal itching in children. Scabies affects skin, while pubic lice live on body hair; they are not ordinary organisms living inside the vagina. Each needs appropriate assessment and treatment, sometimes involving household or sexual contacts. Ask about age, pregnancy and breastfeeding before using an antiparasitic; do not put skin-infestation products inside the vagina.

Why childhood vulvovaginitis is different

Before puberty, delicate lower-estrogen tissues can be easily irritated. Mild nonspecific vulvovaginitis often improves with simple measures and is not automatically an infection needing medicine. Symptoms may recur and often become less frequent as a child grows; puberty does not guarantee that every symptom disappears.

Teach relaxed toileting and gentle front-to-back wiping, change damp clothing and avoid irritants without shaming the child. A clinician may recommend a suitable barrier product. Steroid cream is sometimes considered for particular severe irritation or a diagnosed skin condition, and antibiotics for a supported bacterial cause; neither is an automatic treatment for every child. Persistent night itch, constipation or recurrent symptoms also deserves attention.

Recognising symptoms and concerning changes

Symptoms may include itching, burning, soreness, redness or swelling of the labia and surrounding perineal skin, altered discharge or odour, painful urination and discomfort with sex. Dry, cracked or patchy skin may point toward a skin disorder or hormonal change. Not everyone has every symptom, and discharge colour alone cannot choose the right medicine.

A child with blood-stained or offensive discharge, bleeding, significant pain or persistent symptoms needs medical review; a foreign body or other cause may need specialist assessment. Do not try to remove something from inside the child’s vagina yourself. If there is a disclosure, injury or concern about abuse, seek appropriate urgent paediatric and safeguarding support; symptoms alone do not establish abuse.

Assessment and testing should fit the person

The clinician may ask about timing, discharge, pain, medicines, products, urination, periods, puberty and relevant sexual exposures. An adult examination or swab is discussed with consent; you can ask to stop. Microscopy, culture or molecular tests may help distinguish infections, and urine testing may be needed for urinary symptoms. History or appearance alone can be misleading.

Most mild childhood cases need no tests. Prepubertal children should not have routine internal vaginal examinations or internal swabs. If indicated, a trained clinician can assess externally and take a sample at the entrance for profuse or offensive discharge. Specialist advice is appropriate if the cause is unclear or a foreign body is suspected. A vulval skin biopsy is occasionally used for an uncertain or persistent skin abnormality, not a routine way to identify a vaginal organism.

Treatment is directed at the cause

Treatment may involve an appropriate antibiotic for a diagnosed bacterial condition or STI, an antifungal for confirmed or likely yeast, or an antiviral for herpes. Oral and local treatments are not interchangeable for every cause. Skin disorders may need prescribed steroid treatment, while low-estrogen symptoms may respond to a suitable moisturiser, lubricant or individualized local hormone treatment. An antihistamine may sometimes ease itch, but does not cure an infection.

Ask a clinician or pharmacist before selecting treatment, especially for a child, pregnancy, severe symptoms, recurrence or a first episode. In pregnancy, CDC recommends a topical azole for seven days for candidiasis, not oral fluconazole. Trichomoniasis needs prescribed oral treatment; vaginal metronidazole gel is not sufficient. Complete the prescribed course and follow its specific directions, including medicine interactions and effects on condoms.

Gentle care and the limits of home remedies

Wash the external vulval skin gently with water or a recommended bland emollient and pat dry; do not scrub, over-wash or douche inside the vagina. Avoid perfumed washes, bubble baths, deodorants and products that make symptoms worse. Loose comfortable underwear, changing wet clothes and a clean cool damp cloth against the outside can ease irritation. Do not apply ice directly to skin.

A short plain lukewarm bath may be soothing if comfortable, but avoid hot or prolonged soaking. Tea-tree oil, essential oils and salt mixtures are not established infection cures and may irritate; do not insert them or food. Use a barrier or other cream only as recommended for that area. Home care supports comfort and does not replace appropriate treatment or justify waiting a week with concerning symptoms.

Sex, partner care and avoiding reinfection

If an STI is possible, avoid sex until assessed. For trichomoniasis and certain other STIs, current partners may need treatment even without symptoms; follow infection-specific advice and avoid sex until everyone’s treatment is complete and symptoms have resolved. Sexually active women treated for trichomoniasis should usually be retested around three months. Herpes can be managed, but treatment does not eliminate the virus or all future transmission risk.

Yeast is not usually acquired through sex, and partners do not automatically need treatment. BV is associated with sexual activity and sharing associated bacteria; newer 2025–2026 guidance supports discussion of concurrent treatment for ongoing partners in defined situations, differing from older routine-partner advice. Ask about current local recommendations rather than sharing medicines or assuming every cause needs the same partner treatment. Symptoms or recurrence do not prove infidelity.

Recovery and review

Many causes improve with appropriate care, but the time varies and recurrence is possible. If symptoms fail to improve as expected, change, recur soon after treatment or keep returning, contact the service rather than repeating leftover medicines. Do not wait a fixed week when symptoms are worsening. A new lump, ulcer or persistent skin change also warrants examination.

Record symptom changes, products used, treatment and test results to help reassessment. Diabetes, immune suppression, pregnancy and medication effects may change the plan. Some persistent pain reflects a skin or pain condition rather than continuing infection, and a specialist may help. There is no guarantee that a shop antifungal or hygiene change will settle every episode.

When to seek urgent or emergency help

Seek urgent same-day assessment for fever or chills with symptoms, worsening pelvic or lower abdominal pain, pain in the back or side under the ribs, significant swelling, suspected urinary infection in a child or pregnancy, or visible or suspected blood in urine. Promptly report childhood vaginal bleeding, offensive discharge or significant pain. During pregnancy, discuss new or worsening genital or urinary symptoms with the maternity team; any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy needs immediate advice.

Sudden severe abdominal or pelvic pain, fainting or collapse, confusion, unusual drowsiness, breathing difficulty or severe illness requires immediate emergency care, particularly if pregnancy is possible. These signs may have a cause beyond local irritation, including ectopic pregnancy or serious infection. Do not wait for a cream, home remedy or routine appointment to help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

RCH clinical guidance and parent information distinguish common childhood irritation from targeted infection assessment. Consent, avoiding routine internal examination and cause-directed care remain central.

CDC guidance distinguishes yeast, trichomoniasis and other causes, including pregnancy restrictions and STI partner care. February 2026 New York State BV guidance reflects newer ongoing-partner evidence rather than treating older partner advice as universal.

NHS symptom and skin-care advice and August 2026 Kingston and Richmond biopsy information support gentle care, selective testing and review of persistent skin changes; urgent urinary and pregnancy warnings take priority over home treatment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record symptoms, treatments, test results and questions. It cannot diagnose the cause, assess a child’s safeguarding needs, choose a prescription or replace an examination and urgent care.

When to seek help

Do not douche, insert oils or homemade remedies, or automatically give a child antibiotics, steroids or antifungals. Ask before pregnancy treatment and avoid oral fluconazole in pregnancy. Fever, worsening pelvic pain or urinary warnings need urgent same-day assessment; sudden severe pain, collapse, confusion or breathing difficulty needs emergency care now.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Vulvovaginitis describes irritation or inflammation; infection is only one possible cause.
  • Children and adults need age-appropriate assessment; childhood irritation is not automatically thrush or a bacterial infection.
  • Tests and treatment should match the suspected cause, with consent and no routine internal examination or swabs in prepubertal children.
  • Gentle external care may help comfort; oils, douching and unselected medicines can worsen problems.
  • Fever, worsening pelvic pain, urinary warnings or severe illness need prompt or emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

What causes vulvovaginitis?

Possible causes include irritation, moisture, allergy, skin disease, hormonal changes, bacteria, yeast, STIs and certain parasites. Symptoms overlap, so do not assume one infection from discharge or itch alone.

How is it treated in children and teenagers?

Mild childhood irritation often improves with gentle external care and avoiding irritants. A clinician considers specific causes if symptoms are severe, persistent or recurrent. Antibiotics, steroids and antifungals are not automatic; thrush is uncommon before puberty. Adolescents may need a different assessment according to puberty and relevant exposures.

What symptoms can it cause?

Itch, soreness, swelling, redness, altered or smelly discharge and discomfort with urination or sex may occur. Blood-stained or offensive discharge in a child, fever or worsening pain needs review. Severe pain with collapse or marked illness needs emergency care.

Which home measures are reasonable?

Gentle external washing, drying without rubbing, comfortable clothing and avoiding irritants can help. A cool damp cloth or brief plain lukewarm bath may soothe. Do not douche or insert tea-tree oil, salt mixtures, food or other remedies; they are not proven cures. Do not delay assessment of concerning symptoms.

Does a child need an internal examination or vaginal swab?

Not routinely. Most mild cases need no tests, and prepubertal children should not undergo routine internal examinations or internal swabs. A trained clinician can assess externally and, if appropriate, sample at the entrance or arrange specialist care.

Can I use a yeast medicine I used before?

Past thrush does not prove the current cause. Ask first for pregnancy, a child, new or severe symptoms, recurrence or treatment failure. During pregnancy, current CDC advice uses a topical azole for seven days and avoids oral fluconazole. Persistent symptoms after an over-the-counter course need review.

Does every partner need treatment?

No. It depends on the cause. Current partners need assessment and treatment for trichomoniasis, even without symptoms; yeast does not routinely require partner treatment. For recurrent or symptomatic BV, newer guidance supports discussion of ongoing-partner treatment in defined settings. Follow current local advice and do not share medicines.

When should I seek urgent help?

Fever, worsening pelvic pain, flank pain, significant swelling, urinary infection suspected in a child or pregnancy, or urine blood needs same-day advice. Childhood bleeding or offensive discharge needs prompt assessment. Sudden severe pain, fainting, confusion, breathing difficulty or severe illness needs emergency care now.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
